questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a wet pipe system from a dry pipe system?

options.text: Water is held in the pipes constantly

questions.explanation: Wet pipe systems keep water in the pipes; heat opens a sprinkler head. They are the simplest and fastest, but accidental discharge or leaks can damage electronics.
questions.discriminator_tested: Wet pipe: water always in the pipes.

questions.stem: What is the MAIN drawback of a dry pipe system compared with a wet pipe system?

options.rationale: Correct: gas must escape before water arrives.
That is a wet pipe concern.
Freezing areas are where it's used.

questions.explanation: Dry pipe systems hold pressurized gas; water enters after a head opens. They are used where pipes could freeze, at the cost of slower water delivery.

questions.stem: A data center wants water-based suppression with the lowest chance of accidental discharge. Which BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: detection plus an opened head.
One trigger: a head opening admits water.

questions.explanation: Preaction systems keep the pipes dry; water enters after detection, and a head must then open. The two-step trigger lowers accidental-discharge risk, which makes them common in data centers.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a deluge system from a preaction system?

options.text: Heads open one at a time

questions.explanation: Deluge systems have open heads that discharge water from every head on detection. They deliver massive water flow for high-hazard areas.

questions.stem: A small enclosed room holds a company's core servers and its tape library. Which suppression system BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: no water damage, no residue.
Lowers accidental discharge, but still wets equipment when it fires.

questions.explanation: Clean agent systems use gaseous suppression that leaves no residue. There is no water damage, so they suit equipment rooms.

questions.stem: An old data center still has a working halon system. What BEST describes its status?

options.text: Legacy; no new halon is produced
options.rationale: Correct: production is banned for ozone damage.
True, but it doesn't describe its status.

questions.explanation: Halon is an effective gaseous agent that depletes ozone. Its production is banned (EPA); legacy systems are what remain.

questions.stem: An argon system protects a control room where operators work. What is the MAIN safety concern?

options.rationale: Correct: it works by oxygen reduction.

questions.explanation: Argon is an inert gas that displaces oxygen. It is safe for equipment and works by oxygen reduction, so people must evacuate before discharge.

questions.stem: Which two are chemical clean agents used as halon replacements? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: NAF-S-III is a chemical clean agent developed as a halon replacement. FM-200 (HFC-227ea) is another, widely used in data centers; argon is an inert gas.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAF-S-III and FM-200 are chemical halon replacements.

questions.stem: A data center wants a fast-discharging chemical clean agent, widely used in equipment rooms, that leaves no residue. Which BEST fits?
questions.explanation: FM-200 is a chemical clean agent (HFC-227ea) with fast discharge. It is widely used in data centers and leaves no residue.

questions.stem: A company wants its network core to survive a switch failure without spanning-tree reconvergence, managed as one device. Which BEST fits?

options.rationale: Redundant, but reconverges and is managed separately.

questions.explanation: Switch clustering makes multiple switches operate as one logical switch. A single switch failure doesn't cut connectivity.
questions.discriminator_tested: One logical switch; one failure doesn't cut connectivity.

questions.stem: Hosts use 10.1.1.1 as their default gateway. Given the output below, what is the MOST likely result if R1 fails?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show standby brief
Interface  Grp  Pri  State   Active  Standby   Virtual IP
Gi0/1      10   110  Active  local   10.1.1.3  10.1.1.1

options.rationale: Correct: the standby assumes the virtual gateway.
The virtual IP moves; hosts don't change.
True during failover, but not the key outcome.

questions.explanation: Router redundancy uses redundant routers and multiple paths with a first-hop redundancy protocol such as HSRP. The default gateway stays available.

questions.stem: Which two make a firewall pair's failover transparent to users? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Correct: the standby enforces the same rules.

options.text: Keeping a third unit powered off

questions.explanation: Firewall redundancy uses high-availability pairs (active/standby or active/active) that share session state. State sharing lets sessions survive failover.
questions.discriminator_tested: State sharing lets sessions survive failover.

questions.stem: A web app runs on one server with RAID 1 and dual power supplies. The motherboard fails, and the app goes down. What BEST describes what was missing?

options.rationale: Speeds the repair, but the app still goes down.

questions.explanation: Server redundancy uses clustering, load balancing, redundant power supplies, and RAID to remove single points of failure. The server itself was still one.

questions.stem: A CFO asks for the fastest possible disaster recovery at the lowest possible price. What BEST describes the planner's answer?

options.rationale: True, but they still trade cost against speed.
True, but not the trade-off asked about.

options.text: Site types recover at similar speeds
options.rationale: They range from minutes to weeks.

questions.explanation: Disaster recovery sites are alternate locations to resume operations. The choice is a trade-off between cost and recovery time.
questions.discriminator_tested: Trade-off between cost and recovery time.

questions.stem: A company's disaster recovery plan relies on a cold site. What is the MAIN drawback?

options.text: Equipment must be bought or shipped
options.rationale: True; it's the reason for the delay.

options.text: Data is replicated in real time
options.rationale: A cold site holds no data.

questions.explanation: A cold site provides space with power and connectivity but no equipment or data. It is the cheapest and slowest option (days to weeks).

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a warm site from a hot site?

options.rationale: Correct: partly equipped, data from backups.

options.text: It generally costs less to run
options.rationale: True, but a result of the difference.

options.text: It runs in a cloud provider

questions.explanation: A warm site is partly equipped, with data restored from backups: the middle ground in cost and time. A hot site has near-real-time replication.

questions.stem: A company pays for a fully equipped hot site but replicates data to it once a week. What BEST describes the problem?

options.text: Data at the site can be a week old
options.rationale: Correct: hot sites rely on near-real-time replication.

options.text: It wastes the hot site's cost
options.rationale: A consequence of the stale data.
Replication is what makes them hot.

questions.explanation: A hot site is fully equipped with near-real-time data replication. It is the fastest and most expensive option, and weekly replication defeats its purpose.

questions.stem: A startup with little capital needs a recovery environment that can scale up on demand. Which BEST fits?

options.rationale: Slow, and doesn't scale on demand.

questions.explanation: A cloud site is a recovery environment in a cloud provider, scaled on demand. It has lower upfront cost and is elastic, but depends on connectivity, the provider, and testing.

questions.stem: A team wants no loss of capacity when one node fails and accepts that the second node sits idle until then. Which design BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: the standby takes over at full capacity.
Shares load, but loses capacity on failure.
Can work, but the team chose idle standby.

questions.explanation: Active/active vs active/passive: in active/active every node serves traffic; in active/passive a standby takes over on failure. Active/active shares load but loses capacity on failure; active/passive leaves resources idle.

questions.stem: Which two give a site real internet path diversity? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Same provider, possibly the same path.

questions.explanation: Multiple ISPs and diverse paths mean more than one provider and physically separate routes. Diversity must be physical; two contracts in one conduit still share a failure point.

questions.stem: A team wants to check whether staff know their roles in the recovery plan, with no risk to production systems. Which exercise is BEST?

options.rationale: Hands-on; tests systems more than roles.

questions.explanation: Tabletop exercises have a team talk through a disaster scenario without touching systems. They are discussion only and test roles and plans.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tabletop: discussion only; tests roles and plans.

questions.stem: A company's recovery plan has been talked through in tabletop exercises every year, but never run on real systems. What is MOST clearly missing?

options.rationale: Correct: confirms procedures and systems work.

questions.explanation: Validation tests are hands-on tests that confirm recovery procedures and systems work. They actually exercise systems, unlike a tabletop.

questions.stem: What BEST describes the focus of a disaster recovery plan?
questions.explanation: A disaster recovery plan documents procedures to restore IT systems and data after a disruption. It is IT-focused restoration.

questions.stem: How does a business continuity plan relate to a disaster recovery plan?

options.text: The DRP is one part of the BCP
The BCP is one part of the DRP

questions.explanation: A business continuity plan keeps critical business operations running during and after a disruption. It is broader than IT; the DRP is part of it.
questions.discriminator_tested: BCP is broader; DRP is part of it.
